name: Chamomile extract
lead: Chamomile extract is prepared from the flower heads of daisy-like plants in the Asteraceae family, most often German chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla) and Roman chamomile (Chamaemelum nobile) [1]. It is used in herbal teas and in cosmetics, where it is a common soothing or calming botanical in creams, cleansers and masks.

The flowers contain flavonoids and polyphenols such as apigenin, quercetin and luteolin, along with coumarins [1]. Laboratory studies have reported that chamomile preparations inhibit inflammatory pathways in cultured cells, including COX-2 and prostaglandin release [2].

Human research has focused mainly on oral extracts for anxiety and sleep rather than on skin appearance [3][4]. Wikipedia states that there is no clinical evidence chamomile treats any disease [1]. No trial in the sources reviewed tests chamomile extract for a cosmetic skin outcome.

paras: "Chamomile" is a common name for several species. The two most often used in infusions and extracts are German chamomile and Roman chamomile, while other plants that share the name, such as Anthemis cotula, are not used in the same way [1]. Tea is made by steeping dried flowers in hot water, and the flowers are also used as a flavoring and in soaps, mouthwash and cosmetics [1].

Chamomile is listed in many products marketed for sensitive, reddened or irritated skin, including toners and night creams. Brands generally describe it as calming. In the sources reviewed, the support behind these descriptions is laboratory data on inflammation pathways [2] and a long traditional history of herbal use, not trials in skincare users.

In a study using activated mouse macrophage cells, chamomile treatment reduced release of prostaglandin E2 and was reported to affect the COX-2 enzyme pathway [2]. Other laboratory work has studied the stability and activity of flavonoids isolated from the flowers [5], antiproliferative effects of extracts in human cancer cell lines [6], and effects on colon cells and tissue [7]. These are cell and animal findings and have not been shown to translate into cosmetic effects.

Because chamomile belongs to the Asteraceae family, people allergic to daisies, chrysanthemums, marigolds or ragweed may react to it, and it may worsen pollen allergy [1]. Wikipedia notes possible interactions with some herbs and drugs, advises against combining it with anticoagulants, and says Roman chamomile may cause uterine contractions so pregnant women are advised not to use it [1]. Oral chamomile is generally recognized as safe in the United States [1]. These cautions chiefly concern oral intake.

Human trials of chamomile extract have examined conditions other than skin appearance. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 57 outpatients with mild to moderate generalized anxiety disorder tested an oral chamomile extract against placebo [3]. A randomized placebo-controlled pilot study examined a standardized extract for chronic primary insomnia [4]. A randomized trial compared a preparation of myrrh, chamomile and coffee charcoal with mesalazine for maintaining remission in ulcerative colitis [8]. Registered trials include topical chamomile compared with triamcinolone in oral lichen planus [9] and chamomile in gingivitis [10]. No clinical trial of chamomile extract for skin appearance, redness or irritation was identified in the sources reviewed.

card.summary: A calming flower extract in many soothing creams; lab data on inflammation and oral-use trials, but no skin-appearance trials.
card.aka: Matricaria chamomilla / Matricaria recutita extract, German chamomile, Roman chamomile

quick.overview:
Chamomile extract comes from daisy-like flowers and is a staple soothing ingredient in sensitive-skin products and herbal teas.

Research has mostly tested it by mouth for anxiety and sleep, or in cell and animal inflammation models. Studies of cosmetic skin outcomes are not found in the sources reviewed.
quick.mechanism: Lab work reports that chamomile flavonoids and other constituents dampen inflammatory signaling, including the COX-2 pathway, in cultured cells.
quick.risks: People allergic to daisy-family plants such as ragweed or chrysanthemum may react. Oral use has cautions around anticoagulants and pregnancy.
